new_statements.quote: El acento aparece en la penúltima sílaba en la mayoría de los casos; en la antepenúltima cuando se trata de sustantivos de más de dos sílabas, terminados en el absolutivo -ti o -li y aparece en la última sílaba en determinados paradigmas verbales. new_statements.translation: Stress appears on the penultimate syllable in the majority of cases; on the antepenultimate in nouns of more than two syllables ending in the absolutive -ti or -li, and it appears on the final syllable in certain verbal paradigms. This rather mechanical conditioning of stress has kept us from attributing phonemic value to it. In presenting the material we have written the accent when it falls on the antepenultimate and final syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is penultimate. Two morphologically conditioned departures: (a) nouns of three or more syllables carrying the absolutive suffix -ti/-li are stressed on the antepenult (i.e. the absolutive syllable does not count: kámohti, tékuli, áakawali); (b) certain verb paradigms (and, in the vocabulary, some adverbs) carry final stress (niwí 'I carry', ninamá 'I sell', tremí 'now', payá 'where'). The author treats stress as predictable/non-phonemic and marks it orthographically only in the non-penultimate cases.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in polysyllabic nouns with absolutive -ti/-li; final stress in certain verbal paradigms (vocabulary also shows final-stressed adverbs tremí, unká, nepá, payá). Spanish loans with b, g, f, rr excluded from the phonemic analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement based on elicited citation forms and phrases from three speakers aged 70+ (Jalupa, April-May 1967); accent written in the Spanish-Nahuat vocabulary only when antepenultimate or final. scanned text layer misreads '-ti o -li' as '-ti o -ti'; page image confirms '-ti o -li'.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the náhuat of Jalupa (municipio Jalpa de Méndez, Tabasco), moribund in 1967 (three speakers aged 70+; a few rememberers in Huimango, Cunduacán). The author explicitly distinguishes it from the Boquiapan variety, which he groups with Cupilco (Comalcalco), San Felipe Río Nuevo and Tecominoacán — the area usually meant today by 'Tabasco Nahuatl' nhc (Cupilco). Glottolog 5.1 nonetheless files this article as the sole description under taba1265 and cites it for the languoid's classification (under Isthmus Nahuatl), so the identity matches the Glottolog languoid; note only that the stress statement is for the Jalupa dialect, not Cupilco.

sources.note: p.270 (section FONÉMICA): stress is penultimate in most cases; antepenultimate in nouns of more than two syllables ending in absolutive -ti/-li; final in certain verb paradigms; being 'bastante mecánica' it is not given phonemic value; accent is written in the vocabulary only when antepenultimate or final (e.g. kámohti 'camote', tékuli 'carbón', áakawali 'acahual'; niwí 'llevo', ninamá 'vendo', tremí 'ahora', payá 'dónde').
